name: Peace through strength
summary: Peace through strength holds that a state keeps peace by maintaining military forces, nuclear deterrents and alliances strong and credible enough that adversaries judge aggression a losing bet, while weakness invites attack. In its best-known American form (Reagan and the Republican platforms from 1980) it pursues superiority over the main rival, modernised nuclear forces and strong alliances, and treats arms control as acceptable only if it does not leave the country weaker; scholars equate it with deterrence and often pair it with diplomacy.

notFound.work: Houston, Invitation to Peace Studies (Oxford University Press, 2015), pp. 24-25, the scholarly passage on the phrase

tried.how: searched reference/text by title and author
searched for a publisher preview of the book

scope: The doctrine named by the phrase, as the sources that define it present it: a strong, credible military (nuclear and conventional) and alliances that deter aggression and so preserve peace (s1, s2), in the form Reagan and the Republican platforms from 1980 gave it (s1, s3, s4, s6). It excludes the policies of other users of the phrase, the Reagan Doctrine on aiding anti-communist insurgents, and domestic policy; the texts speak chiefly about defence, nuclear forces, alliances and arms control.

keyFigures.role: US president who made peace through strength a mainstay of his foreign policy
keyFigures.quote: Republican presidential candidate Ronald Reagan cemented the phrase during his 1980 campaign.

quotes.text: A well-appointed military improves diplomacy with adversaries, strengthens our alliances, signals credibility and resolve, deters aggression, and enhances national morale.

notes: Themes searched: defence and force structure, nuclear forces, alliances and bases, arms control, conscription and manpower, interventions, trade and technology exports, aid, the UN, and the economy and domestic themes (nothing in the defining sources). The doctrine speaks almost only to military and alliance questions, so most statements are null. Sources about the Reagan Doctrine, the 1980 platform's non-defence sections and other users of the phrase (Chamberlain, Taiwan, France) were not used for answers. Critics (Bacevich, Morrison, Hatfield) were not used. The 1980 platform answers rest on its HCR 306 strategy text and defence sections that adopt the strategy by name.
